Plant the Moon - Final Report 
By CosmoLab 
Eddie Yang & Annie Yang 
 
1.​ Background 
In the Spring 2025 Plant the Moon Challenge, we investigated the effect of different soil types on the growth 
performance of four plant species: spinach, tomato, bell pepper, and lettuce. These plants were selected to 
represent a range of growth patterns, including leafy vegetables and fruit-bearing crops, each with different 
nutrient and environmental requirements for survival. 
2. Project Hypothesis 
We hypothesized that plants grown in Garden soil would perform significantly better—in terms of height, 
survival rate, and overall growth trend—than those grown in lunar simulant soil, due to the Garden soil’s 
higher nutrient content, better water retention, and more favorable physical properties. 
We also expected that plants grown in the 50/50 Earth-lunar soil mix would demonstrate intermediate 
growth, with better results than pure lunar simulant but poorer performance than Garden soil alone. 
Furthermore, we hypothesized that different plant species would respond differently to soil conditions, 
with fast-growing leafy vegetables like spinach and lettuce being more resilient in low-nutrient substrates 
compared to fruit-bearing crops like tomatoes and bell peppers. 
3. Experimental Variables 
●​ Independent Variable: The type of soil used for growing the plants—Garden soil (Miracle-Gro), a 1:1 
Earth-lunar mix, and pure lunar simulant. 
●​ Dependent Variables: Plant height (cm), survival rate, growth trend and peak timing, standard 
deviation of height. 
●​ Control Variables: Planting date (Feb 12, 2025), pot size, watering volume and frequency, lighting 
duration and intensity, environmental temperature and humidity, seed source, and measurement 
methods.

4. Controls 
The Garden soil group served as the control condition, using 100% Miracle-Gro Garden Soil All Purpose. No 
added fertilizers or soil supplements were used in any group. All groups were watered with the same volume and 
frequency using bottled distilled water. The lighting schedule was fixed at 12 hours per day using consistent 
artificial grow lights. Temperature was maintained between 22–25°C in a stable indoor environment. 
Each plant species (spinach, tomato, bell pepper, lettuce) was planted using identical 4-inch plastic pots in three 
soil types. Seeds were planted on the same day, and measured with the same ruler every 5 days. Pots were 
arranged uniformly to ensure equal exposure to light and air. 
5. Experimental Design and Procedures 
This experiment was designed to evaluate the growth of four edible plant species under three distinct soil 
conditions. The study included a total of 48 pots—4 plant species × 3 soil types × 4 pots per group. All seeds 
were planted on February 12, 2025 (Day 0), and the experiment continued for 60 days, ending on April 12, 
2025. 
Each pot was filled with one of the three soil treatments: 
●​ Garden Soil: 100% Miracle-Gro Garden Soil All Purpose. 
●​ Mix Soil: 50% Garden soil and 50% NASA lunar simulant by volume. 
●​ Lunar Soil: 100% NASA-provided lunar simulant. 
For each plant-soil combination, four pots were used, labeled, and tracked separately. Spinach and lettuce were 
planted with 2–4 seeds per pot; tomato and bell pepper were planted with 1–2 seeds due to their larger growth 
form. After germination, seedlings were thinned to 1–2 per pot, depending on the plant's strength and 
uniformity. 
Containers and Setup: All plants were grown in uniform 4-inch plastic pots placed in trays to control water 
drainage. Each pot was labeled clearly by plant species, soil type, and replicate number (e.g., SP-E1 for 
Spinach-Earth-Pot 1). Pots were arranged in a randomized block pattern under a full-spectrum LED grow light 
system providing 12 hours of light per day. 
Environmental Controls: Temperature was monitored daily and maintained between 22–25°C. Humidity was 
not artificially controlled but kept stable through room insulation. Plants were watered twice per week 
(Mondays and Thursdays) using bottled distilled water, and measured using graduated cylinders to ensure equal 
volume. Each pot received approximately 25–30 mL of water per session.

Moisture Management: To reduce evaporation during germination, pots were loosely covered with plastic 
wrap until sprouts reached the surface. The soil was not fertilized or supplemented in any group. To prevent 
compaction in the lunar and mixed soil pots, a wooden skewer was used to gently aerate the soil once per week. 
Measurement Procedures: Plant height was measured every five days using a clear plastic ruler, from soil level 
to the tallest visible part of the plant. Measurements were taken at the same time of day by the same person to 
maintain consistency. Plant health indicators—such as leaf color, stem strength, and signs of wilting or 
death—were recorded alongside numerical data. 
In the event of early death or halted growth, the final measurement for the plant was marked and used in survival 
analysis. All data were compiled into spreadsheets and used to calculate average height and standard deviation 
across each group. 
This experimental setup allowed for the isolated evaluation of soil type on plant growth, with a standardized, 
repeatable procedure across all species. 
6. Results and Analysis 
6.1 Spinach 
Spinach demonstrated varied growth and survival trends across the three soil types over the 60-day experiment. 
The chart illustrates average plant height with standard deviation error bars, while the germination rate chart 
captures initial seed performance. 
Spinach planted in mixed soil (50% lunar simulant + 50% garden soil) showed the fastest initial growth 
and the highest germination rate (100%). These plants reached their peak height of approximately 8.0–8.1 
cm between Day 25–30, outperforming both the lunar and garden soil groups during this phase. However, 
beginning on Day 35, their growth plateaued and started to decline. By Day 50, all plants in the mixed soil 
group had died. This suggests that although the nutrient blend or initial structure of the mix supported rapid 
germination and early development, it could not sustain long-term spinach growth—possibly due to root 
limitations, soil compaction, or nutrient imbalance over time. 
Spinach grown in lunar soil (100% simulant) had the second-highest germination rate (over 90%) and a similar 
early growth trend to the mixed group, peaking around 7.2 cm at Day 25–30. However, these plants started 
showing stress signs earlier, with a visible decline beginning around Day 35, and complete die-off by Day 45. 
The lower height plateau and shorter survival period suggest that lunar simulant, while not immediately toxic to 
spinach, lacks the structure or nutrients needed for continued development. 
In contrast, spinach planted in pure garden soil had the lowest germination rate (under 50%), possibly due 
to soil compaction or high moisture retention. However, for the plants that germinated, growth was steady and 
sustained. The average height reached 9 cm by Day 45, the highest overall, and remained relatively stable

through Day 60, even as other groups declined. This indicates that while fewer plants germinated in the garden 
soil, those that did had the best long-term growth and survival. (See Table 1, Figure 1.1 and 1.2) 
In summary, spinach grew tallest and lived longest in garden soil, showed strong early performance in mixed 
soil but declined sharply after Day 35, and experienced early die-off in lunar soil. This suggests that lunar 
simulant—even when mixed with Garden soil—may provide an initial growth boost but cannot maintain 
spinach health long-term. Garden soil, though slower to start, remains the most reliable medium for sustained 
spinach cultivation. 
6.2 Tomato 
Tomato growth results demonstrated clear differences among the three soil conditions. As expected, plants 
grown in 100% garden soil exhibited the most robust and consistent growth pattern, reaching an 
average height of over 10 cm by Day 60. This group showed steady upward growth throughout the 
experiment, with a relatively high germination rate (over 60%). The increasing standard deviation toward the 
end of the 60 days suggests some individual variation in plant height as tomatoes matured and possibly 
competed for nutrients and light. 
In contrast, plants grown in 50/50 lunar and garden mixed soil performed significantly worse, 
plateauing early around Day 30 at an average height of approximately 5.3 cm, and showing little to no 
further growth thereafter. Surprisingly, their germination rate was the second highest (around 30%), 
indicating that while seeds could sprout in the mixed soil, continued growth was likely hindered by poor soil 
structure or nutrient imbalance. The relatively flat growth curve and low variation indicate uniform but 
stunted development. 
Tomato plants in pure lunar simulant soil initially showed slow growth and a lower germination rate 
(around 20%), but those that germinated displayed gradual and steady growth, surpassing the mixed soil 
group after Day 35 and reaching an average height of over 8 cm by Day 60. This suggests that, despite the low 
initial success rate, tomatoes that did manage to establish roots in lunar simulant soil adapted reasonably well 
over time. Notably, none of the plants in this group showed die-off, and the standard deviation bars 
remained moderate throughout the experiment. (See Table 2, Figure 2.1 and 2.2) 
These findings emphasize species-specific adaptation: tomatoes appear to be relatively resilient, and with 
proper water and light management, they can tolerate low-nutrient conditions better than expected. However, 
the garden soil remains the most supportive environment for optimal tomato development in both 
germination and long-term growth. 
6.3 Bell Pepper 
Bell pepper plants showed the most dramatic differences in growth and germination performance across the 
three soil types.

As hypothesized, garden soil provided the most supportive environment for bell pepper growth. Plants in this 
group exhibited continuous and steady vertical development throughout the 60 days, reaching an average height 
of approximately 9.4 cm by Day 60. The growth pattern was smooth and consistent, and variability in plant 
height remained moderate, as indicated by the relatively uniform standard deviation bars. This suggests that 
garden soil offered stable nutrient availability and moisture retention, allowing for sustained growth over time. 
In contrast, plants grown in the 50/50 mixed soil showed limited and early growth, peaking at around 3.3 
cm between Day 30 and Day 35. After this peak, growth stagnated and began to decline steadily, with most 
plants dying off by Day 60. Interestingly, while the germination rate in the mixed soil was slightly better than in 
lunar soil, the plants failed to maintain viability long-term. This could be attributed to potential issues in the 
structural integrity or nutrient balance of the mixed soil, such as compaction or poor aeration. 
Bell peppers grown in lunar simulant soil showed the lowest overall performance. Although some seedlings 
germinated (about 12.5% germination rate), their growth was slow and shallow. Peak height only reached 2.8 
cm around Day 25, and a clear downward trend started soon after. All lunar group bell pepper plants died by 
around Day 50. The early decline suggests that the lunar simulant lacked key nutrients or retained insufficient 
moisture to support the bell peppers’ development. (See Table 3, Figure 3.1 and 3.2) 
Overall, these results reinforce that bell peppers are particularly sensitive to suboptimal growing conditions. 
Unlike spinach and tomatoes, which exhibited at least partial adaptation to lunar or mixed media, bell peppers 
only thrived in Garden soil, making them a poor candidate for lunar agriculture without significant soil 
enhancement strategies. 
6.4 Lettuce 
Lettuce showed notable differences in growth patterns and survival depending on soil type. As hypothesized, 
lettuce grown in Garden soil produced the most consistent and prolonged growth. Plants in this group steadily 
increased in height, reaching a peak average of approximately 6.4 cm around Day 50, and maintaining healthy 
foliage until the end of the 60 days. This group had the lowest overall plant loss and maintained strong 
performance throughout the study, indicating that Garden soil provides a stable, nutrient-rich, and 
moisture-retaining environment ideal for lettuce cultivation. 
Unexpectedly, lettuce grown in mixed soil (50% Garden soil + 50% lunar simulant) outperformed both Earth 
and lunar soils during the first 20 days. The plants reached their peak average height of ~4.7 cm by Day 20, 
indicating an early surge of growth, possibly due to initial nutrient availability or favorable physical conditions in 
the mixed medium. However, after Day 25, growth began to decline steadily. By Day 45, all lettuce plants in 
mixed soil had died, suggesting that the soil mixture may have failed to retain moisture or lacked consistent 
nutrients to support sustained growth. 
Lunar soil lettuce growth was limited and short-lived. Though some plants germinated and reached moderate 
height (~4 cm by Day 25), growth was generally slower and peaked earlier than the other two groups. After Day

30, a continuous decline began, with a complete die-off by Day 50. The plants in this group showed higher 
variability, as reflected in the large standard deviation bars, likely due to uneven conditions in the simulant 
medium. This supports the notion that lunar regolith alone is insufficient for sustained lettuce growth without 
supplementation. 
In terms of germination rates, lettuce in Garden soil showed the highest rate (~42%), followed by lunar soil 
(~22%), with mixed soil (~17%) performing the worst. This outcome suggests that while the lunar simulant 
has a limited capacity to support germination and early development, the mixed soil group might have 
introduced adverse conditions—perhaps structural compaction or chemical imbalance—that negatively 
impacted both germination and survival. (See Table 4, Figure 4.1 and 4.2) 
Overall, these results reinforce the hypothesis that Garden soil is the most suitable growing medium for 
lettuce. While mixed soil may offer a short-term growth advantage, it is not viable for full growth cycles. Lettuce 
grown in lunar simulant alone had poor performance both in growth and germination, highlighting the 
importance of soil composition for long-term plant development. 
7. Conclusion 
Our hypothesis was that garden soil would provide the most favorable conditions for all four plants due to its 
higher organic content, nutrients, and better water retention compared to mixed or lunar simulant soils. This 
hypothesis was largely supported, though with several interesting variations among plant types. 
For spinach, we observed that the mixed soil group had the highest germination rate and fastest early 
growth, peaking earlier than all other groups. However, these plants experienced a sharp decline and complete 
die-off around Day 45, suggesting that while the mixed soil supported early growth, it could not sustain the 
plants long-term. Garden soil, in contrast, supported slower but more steady growth, reaching the highest 
average height (~9 cm) and lasting through Day 60. Lunar soil allowed germination but showed significantly 
stunted growth and early death by Day 45. These results suggest that spinach can be initially stimulated by 
mixed soil, but only garden soil supports healthy, sustained growth. 
Lettuce plants showed a different pattern. While mixed soil again led to early height gains (peaking around Day 
20–25), plants began to decline soon afterward, with complete die-off by Day 45. In contrast, garden soil 
supported gradual and continuous growth, peaking near Day 50–55 around 6.7 cm, and remained viable 
until Day 60. Lunar soil had limited germination success and very poor growth, with most plants dying by Day 
40. These results indicate that lettuce is more tolerant of gradual nutrient release, and garden soil provides 
the best overall environment. 
For tomatoes, garden soil was the most successful, with strong germination and continuous upward growth 
throughout the experiment, surpassing 10 cm by Day 60. Surprisingly, lunar soil supported slow but steady 
growth, outperforming mixed soil by the end of the experiment. Mixed soil resulted in early stagnation and

limited development, plateauing under 6 cm. This suggests that tomatoes are particularly sensitive to 
inconsistencies in soil structure or nutrient delivery, which may be present in the 50/50 mixed medium. 
Bell pepper plants showed the lowest performance overall, with poor germination across all soil types, 
especially in lunar simulant. However, for the few that did germinate, garden soil once again enabled 
continuous growth, reaching around 9.4 cm by Day 60. Both mixed and lunar soils led to early plateauing 
(around Day 30–35) and complete die-off before the end of the experiment. Bell peppers appear to be 
particularly sensitive to nutrient-poor or poorly structured soils and only thrive in more enriched 
environments like garden soil. 
Across all four species, we observed that mixed soil often provided a short-term boost in growth but failed 
to sustain plants long-term. Garden soil consistently provided the best balance of germination success, 
growth rate, and long-term survival. Lunar soil, while capable of supporting limited growth in tomatoes and 
spinach early on, generally resulted in poor plant health and high mortality. 
8. Discussion and Future Recommendations 
This experiment highlights the critical role of soil composition in plant germination, growth trajectory, and 
survival. While our initial assumption that garden soil would be the most effective growing medium was mostly 
validated, the dynamic responses across plant species underscore that soil performance is not one-size-fits-all. 
One notable finding is that mixed soil (50% garden soil + 50% lunar simulant) appeared to promote early 
germination and accelerated growth in spinach and lettuce, yet failed to sustain those plants beyond Day 45. 
This suggests a possible initial nutrient burst or looser soil texture that encourages early development but lacks 
the nutrient stability or structure needed for long-term health. Future studies could explore optimizing the ratio 
of soil to lunar simulant or incorporating slow-release organic fertilizers to extend viability in this medium. 
Tomatoes performed better than expected in pure lunar soil, showing steady upward growth despite poor 
germination. This indicates that tomato plants may be more adaptable to challenging environments, particularly 
if conditions such as moisture and light are well maintained. However, the low germination rate still poses a 
barrier. A potential strategy would be to start tomato seedlings in nutrient-rich soil, then transplant them to 
lunar substrate once established. 
Bell peppers, while generally underperforming across all soil types, clearly require more nutrient-dense and 
stable environments to thrive. Their poor performance in mixed and lunar soils, even at the germination stage, 
suggests that they are less resilient and not well-suited for harsh growing mediums. Future trials might 
experiment with pre-soaking seeds, using seed starters, or supplementing with micronutrients known to aid in 
germination and root development. 
An additional insight came from observing plant decline trends after peak growth. Both spinach and lettuce 
grown in mixed or lunar soils often showed rapid senescence post-Day 30–35, while garden soil plants generally

plateaued or declined gradually. This points to soil longevity and nutrient retention as key factors in sustaining 
life cycles and emphasizes the importance of re-fertilization schedules or soil amendment strategies in long-term 
lunar agriculture planning. 
For future experiments, we recommend the following: 
●​ Conduct more granular soil analysis, particularly of the mixed and lunar simulant, to identify which 
nutrients may be missing or imbalanced.​
 
●​ Test staggered fertilizer additions, such as a second dose of nitrogen or phosphorus at the 3-week mark, 
to sustain growth beyond the initial surge.​
 
●​ Try other soil additives (e.g., compost, vermiculite, or kelp meal) to improve soil structure and water 
retention in lunar simulants.​
 
●​ Use pre-germinated or nursery-grown seedlings for more sensitive species like bell peppers to improve 
establishment success.​
 
This experiment serves as a strong baseline for understanding how various plants react to lunar simulant soils 
and suggests that tailored soil management will be essential for future space-based agriculture. While spinach 
and lettuce may be useful as quick-growth leafy crops, tomatoes may serve as reliable long-term producers, and 
bell peppers might require significant adaptation support before being considered viable candidates for 
extraterrestrial farming.
